summary: An applicability statement for Classless Inter-Domain Routing, a way to slow the growth of routing tables and the use of new IP network numbers. It says what is needed to implement CIDR in the Internet. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of listing every house in a big city separately, you list whole neighborhoods. This memo says how routers should do that.

subtitle: An applicability statement for Classless Inter-Domain Routing to slow growth of routing tables and conserve IP address space.

tldr.problem: The Internet is running out of class-B network addresses because they are either too small (class-C) or too large (class-B), leading to wasteful allocation and explosive growth of routing tables.
tldr.mechanism: CIDR allows routers to aggregate multiple network routes into a single prefix, reducing routing table size and slowing IP address exhaustion.
tldr.outcome: This standard was selected as the solution for short-term routing problems and is now historic as IPv6 addresses have become the long-term solution.

today: RFC 1517 is Historic. CIDR was a critical interim solution that helped the Internet continue growing through the 1990s. However, it has been superseded by IPv6, which provides a vastly larger address space and eliminates the need for address conservation techniques.

sections.title: The Scaling Crisis
sections.content: By 1993, the Internet faced critical scaling problems. Class-B addresses were nearly exhausted, yet class-C addresses (supporting only 254 hosts) were too small for most organizations. As a result, sites allocated multiple class-B addresses even when they used only a fraction of the addresses, wasting the limited address space. The routing tables in Internet routers grew exponentially as new networks were added. Both problems threatened the Internet's ability to continue growing.
sections.plainLanguage: Streets were getting too crowded with houses, and the system for delivering mail could not keep up with the growth.

sections.title: How CIDR Works
sections.content: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) solves these problems by allowing routers to treat multiple network addresses as a single routing entry. Instead of listing every class-C network separately, CIDR lets an organization use a single IP prefix to cover multiple networks. This aggregation dramatically reduces routing table size while making better use of address space. CIDR does not require all Internet domains to adopt it immediately, but backbone and transit domains are required to implement it fully.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of listing each house, list the whole block. A router lists one route that covers many networks instead of many separate routes.

sections.title: Implementation Requirements
sections.content: This applicability statement requires Internet backbone and transit domains to fully implement CIDR to ensure the growth of router resources stays ahead of network growth. Non-backbone domains are strongly recommended to implement CIDR as well to reduce routing information overhead. CIDR requires routers to support inter-domain routing protocols that can handle IP address prefixes. Domains may continue to use non-CIDR addressing, but they will rely on default routes from CIDR-capable parts of the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The main post offices must use CIDR. Other offices should too. Some offices can stay old-fashioned if they are willing to ask for directions.

references.text: Rekhter, Y., and T. Li, An Architecture for IP Address Allocation with CIDR, RFC 1518, September 1993.
